sections.title: Framing the GI history: symptom screen, alarm features and background

blocks.text: A GI history screens a fixed list of symptoms, then explores whichever is the presenting one. Screen for **abdominal pain, appetite and weight change, early satiety, nausea and vomiting, heartburn and regurgitation, waterbrash, dysphagia, change in bowel habit, bloating, bleeding, jaundice (with dark urine and pale stools), itch, lethargy and fever**. Kumar groups the common presentations as a "top ten": acute upper GI bleed, dysphagia, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, malabsorption, diarrhoea, iron-deficiency anaemia, rectal bleeding, constipation and tenesmus.

blocks.title: Alarm (red-flag) features: these trigger urgent investigation
items: Davidson (dyspepsia, Box 21.15): **anaemia, weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, and a palpable abdominal mass**
**New dyspepsia after age 55** needs endoscopy; any alarm feature means **urgent** endoscopy. Younger patients with no alarm features: test and treat for _H. pylori_
Talley (reflux): dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, melaena or haematemesis. Without these, reflux can be diagnosed from typical symptoms alone
Kumar: progressive weight loss, anorexia and symptoms of anaemia from chronic blood loss suggest malignancy
Dysphagia, bleeding and weight loss always need investigation

blocks.text: The books list different alarm features. Talley names four for reflux (dysphagia, weight loss, melaena, haematemesis). **Davidson's list is wider: it adds anaemia, vomiting and a palpable mass.** In the exam, use Davidson's list and the over-55 rule for new dyspepsia.

blocks.title: Drug history: what to ask about and why
rows: C. difficile diarrhoea; some cause cholestasis
Always ask: patients often leave them out

blocks.title: Past, family and social history
items: Past history: earlier GI or autoimmune disease and any abdominal surgery
Family history: colon cancer and familial polyps, IBD, coeliac disease
Family history of jaundice, anaemia, splenectomy or cholecystectomy suggests a haemolytic anaemia or familial hyperbilirubinaemia
Social history: smoking and alcohol (quantified; see the alcohol history in section 3)

blocks.text: IBS is a **positive diagnosis made from the history**. Rome IV criteria: recurrent abdominal pain on **at least 1 day a week, on average, over the last 3 months**, with **2 or more** of the following: linked to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form. The diagnosis requires that alarm features are absent.

blocks.note: Dyspepsia algorithm: alarm features or new symptoms after 55 lead to endoscopy; otherwise test and treat for H. pylori

sections.title: Abdominal pain, vomiting, reflux and dysphagia

blocks.title: Characterising abdominal pain
rows: Dull or burning epigastric pain that comes in episodes; food or antacids ease it somewhat; may wake the patient at night. History cannot tell gastric from duodenal ulcer
Steady epigastric pain, often through to the back; sitting forward helps; vomiting is common
Severe, **constant** epigastric or RUQ pain lasting hours, starting unpredictably. Moves to the RUQ and worsens if cholecystitis follows
Periumbilical colic every **2–3 min**, with vomiting, constipation and distension
Colic every **10–15 min**, with distension and constipation

blocks.title: Other pain clues
items: Radiation to the **back**: pancreas or a penetrating peptic ulcer. To the **shoulder**: diaphragmatic irritation. To the **throat**: oesophageal reflux or spasm
Restless, rolling patient: colic. Patient lying motionless: peritonitis

Davidson's four types of pain: **visceral** (stretch, poorly localised, midline), **parietal** (sharp, well localised), **referred** (e.g. gallbladder pain felt at the shoulder tip or back) and **psychogenic**

Acute abdomen: inflammatory pain builds over hours and localises once the parietal peritoneum is involved. Perforation pain starts abruptly and is severe. Obstruction pain is colicky; continuous pain between spasms suggests added inflammation

blocks.text: **Biliary colic is not colicky.** It is a steady, severe pain that lasts hours. Do not exclude gallstones because the pain does not come in waves.

blocks.title: Nausea and vomiting
items: Vomiting **more than 1 hour after meals**, or vomitus containing old food: gastric outlet obstruction or gastroparesis
Projectile vomiting closely tied to meals suggests a pyloric stricture
**Early-morning vomiting before food**: pregnancy, alcoholism, raised intracranial pressure

Chronic causes: pregnancy; drugs (digoxin, opiates, dopamine agonists, chemotherapy); outlet obstruction; gastroparesis (diabetes, after surgery); hepatobiliary disease; alcohol; eating disorders; raised ICP
Anorexia with weight loss suggests malignancy (or depression). Weight loss despite a **good appetite** suggests malabsorption or a hypermetabolic state such as thyrotoxicosis

blocks.text: **Rumination is not vomiting.** After eating, food comes back up into the mouth effortlessly and is spat out or swallowed again. Patients often call it "vomiting", so ask them to describe an episode.

**Heartburn** is a retrosternal burning that rises toward the throat after meals, on bending or on lying flat, and is eased by antacids. More than once a week suggests GORD, and acid regurgitation makes reflux very likely. Up to **half** of reflux patients have atypical symptoms instead: chest pain, belching, bad breath, chronic cough or sore throat. Kumar notes that reflux symptoms are worsened by both eating and posture, and that early satiety can point to gastric cancer.
If "heartburn" spreads to the **left arm or jaw**, think of myocardial ischaemia. **Waterbrash** (a sudden flood of salty or tasteless saliva into the mouth) is not regurgitation.

blocks.title: Dysphagia: reading the history
rows: Trouble starting a swallow, choking, coughing, nasal regurgitation
Food "sticks" after swallowing, felt in the chest
Intermittent bolus impaction in an atopic patient (asthma, hay fever)
Odynophagia: severe oesophagitis (Candida, HSV), peptic ulceration, caustic injury
Lump in the throat with no real swallowing problem

blocks.text: Kumar's rule: a high sensation (mouth or pharynx), worse with **liquids**, with speech involvement suggests a neurological cause. A low (chest) sensation, worse with large solid boluses, suggests a structural cause. Achalasia also affects liquids, because it is a motility disorder, not a fixed blockage.

Dysphagia **always** needs urgent investigation. Endoscopy comes first because it allows biopsy and dilatation. Take biopsies even if the mucosa looks normal, to look for eosinophilic oesophagitis. Barium swallow or videofluoroscopy, then manometry, follow if needed.

blocks.note: Dysphagia work-up: oropharyngeal (videofluoroscopy, neurological assessment) vs oesophageal (endoscopy and biopsy, then manometry or barium)

sections.title: Bowel habit, GI bleeding, jaundice and the liver and alcohol history

blocks.title: Types of diarrhoea
rows: Small, frequent stools with blood or mucus
Pale, very offensive stools that float and are hard to flush; >7 g fat per 24 h

blocks.title: Bowel habit red flags and clues
items: **Nocturnal** diarrhoea suggests an organic cause. Blood, mucus or pus suggests colonic disease. Weight loss and fever are alarm features
Recent antibiotics: think _C. difficile_. Recent travel: think _Giardia_

Constipation: fewer than three stools a week, hard stools or difficult evacuation. Drug causes: codeine, antidepressants, aluminium or calcium antacids. Metabolic causes: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes, hypokalaemia
A **recent change in bowel habit** may signal colonic cancer. A persistent unexplained loosening of stool deserves the same concern
Straining, a feeling of anal blockage or self-digitation suggests a pelvic floor evacuation disorder or anorectal disease
**Tenesmus** (feeling of incomplete emptying) suggests anorectal pathology such as a tumour

blocks.title: Bleeding: what the description tells you
rows: Brisk bleeding at or above the duodenum; an emergency
Slower upper GI bleeding, still serious
Clear vomiting first, then blood after repeated retching
Usually an upper GI source, occasionally the right colon; an emergency
Small amounts of bright blood on the paper or on the stool surface

blocks.title: Upper GI bleed: bedside assessment
items: Look for shock: tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria
Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease (possible varices) and serious comorbidity
A **raised urea with a normal creatinine** suggests a large bleed (blood absorbed as protein)
**Blatchford score of 2 or less** means low risk
Exclude blood from the nose, a tooth socket or haemoptysis before calling it haematemesis

blocks.title: Commonest bleeding sources
rows: Peptic ulcer 35–50% (often a painless chronic duodenal ulcer), gastric erosions 10–20%, oesophagitis 10%, Mallory–Weiss 5%, varices 2–9%, cancer 2%
Angiodysplasia, diverticular disease, colonic cancer or polyp, haemorrhoids or fissure

blocks.text: Diverticula are **commoner in the left colon**, but diverticular **bleeding more often comes from the right side**.

blocks.title: Jaundice and liver history
items: **Dark urine with pale stools**: obstructive or cholestatic jaundice, because bilirubin does not reach the gut. Cholestatic itch tends to be worse over the limbs
Jaundice with **normal-coloured urine**: think haemolysis

Checklist: fever (cholangitis), weight loss (cancer), alcohol, injecting drugs, tattoos, transfusion, new drugs, sexual risk, travel to hepatitis A areas, HBV vaccination, IBD (PSC), prior biliary surgery, occupation, family history
Viral hepatitis risk: childhood in an endemic country, shared needles or unsafe tattoos, unprotected high-risk sex

Liver disease is often silent early, so the history must establish **risk factors**: alcohol, drugs, viral exposure, metabolic syndrome (obesity, diabetes, gout, high cholesterol), heart failure, autoimmune disease, family history of haemochromatosis
Chronic liver disease symptoms: fatigue and anorexia, RUQ ache, abdominal swelling, ankle swelling, variceal bleeding, itch, gynaecomastia or loss of libido or amenorrhoea, confusion (encephalopathy)
Itch from cholestasis is often an **early** symptom of primary biliary cholangitis

blocks.title: The alcohol history
items: Quantify: drink type and strength, daily units, alcohol-free days, binges and duration
Dependence: morning drinking, inability to stop, guilt, others worried, injuries
**CAGE**: felt you should **C**ut down? **A**nnoyed by criticism? **G**uilty? **E**ye-opener in the morning?
**AUDIT** (WHO): 10 scored questions; **8 or more** indicates harmful use
UK guidance (DoH 2016): **no more than 14 units a week** for men and women, spread over 3 or more days

blocks.text: Patients often **under-report** alcohol intake and dependence. Ask tactfully and without judgement.

sections.title: Setting up the exam, general inspection and peripheral signs

blocks.text: Lay the patient **flat on one pillow** with the abdomen fully exposed, and offer a chaperone. Work from the periphery inward: general inspection, hands, arms, face, lymph nodes, chest, then abdomen (**inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate**), groin and legs. Finish with a rectal exam, urinalysis and temperature. Davidson adds an early look at distress, fever, hydration and nutrition. Kumar adds checking pulse and blood pressure for shock in acute bleeding.

blocks.title: Peripheral signs and what they suggest
rows: Cirrhosis (up to one-third, possibly pulmonary AV shunting), IBD, coeliac disease
Bruising, petechiae, scratch marks, spider naevi
Clotting failure or low platelets, cholestatic itch, chronic liver disease
Jaundice, conjunctival pallor, parotid swelling, fetor hepaticus
Pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum; pitting oedema

blocks.text: Why bruising in liver disease? The liver makes all the clotting factors **except factor VIII**, so synthesis fails in cirrhosis. In **obstructive jaundice**, vitamin K is poorly absorbed, so factors **II, VII, IX and X** fall. **Petechiae** point instead to thrombocytopenia (alcohol or hypersplenism).

Spider naevi are telangiectases with a central arteriole and small vessels radiating out. Palmar erythema reflects a hyperdynamic circulation. A cluster of jaundice, oedema, ascites, spider naevi, gynaecomastia and easy bleeding means **liver cell failure**.
A **normal examination does not exclude advanced chronic liver disease**: many patients have very few signs. Acute liver disease may show only jaundice and an enlarged liver.

blocks.note: How to elicit asterixis (arms out, wrists extended); petechiae

sections.title: The abdomen: inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation

blocks.title: Inspection
items: Generalised distension, the "F"s: fat, fluid (ascites), fetus, flatus, faeces, a "filthy" big tumour, phantom pregnancy. In ascites the umbilicus is shallow or everted and points down
Dilated veins below the umbilicus: **portal hypertension** (caput Medusae) drains **away from the umbilicus**, down toward the legs. **IVC obstruction** drains **upward** toward the head
Sister Joseph nodule: a metastatic deposit at the umbilicus
**Cullen's sign** (bluish periumbilical discoloration): extensive haemoperitoneum or acute pancreatitis. **Grey Turner's sign** (flank discoloration): severe acute pancreatitis
Wide purple striae suggest Cushing's syndrome

blocks.text: **Guarding** is voluntary and relaxes with reassurance. **Rigidity** is constant and involuntary, always comes with tenderness, and means **peritonitis**. Peritonitis gives guarding, rebound, rigidity and a silent abdomen. Palpate the tender area last.

blocks.title: Describing a mass
items: Site, tenderness, measured size and shape, surface, edge, consistency, movement with breathing, pulsation, and whether you can get above it
Right iliac fossa: caecal cancer, Crohn's mass, appendix abscess
Left iliac fossa: sigmoid cancer, faeces, diverticular mass
Epigastrium: gastric or pancreatic cancer, aortic aneurysm

blocks.title: Palpating the organs
rows: Start in the RIF; move up 1–2 cm with each breath out. Upper border at the 6th intercostal space (MCL); normal span <13 cm (clinical estimates read 2–5 cm low)
A palpable edge is very specific (100%) but insensitive (48%) for enlargement; LR+ 2.5, LR− 0.5. Cirrhotic liver may be small

Pulsatile: tricuspid regurgitation. Tender: hepatitis, rapid swelling (heart failure, Budd–Chiari), abscess, cholangitis. Massive: metastases, alcoholic fatty liver, myeloproliferative disease, right heart failure, HCC
Start below the umbilicus and move toward the left costal margin; if not felt, roll the patient onto the right side
Palpable only when about 1.5–2 times enlarged; a palpable spleen has LR+ 9.6
Murphy's sign: patient stops breathing in as the inflamed gallbladder meets your hand under the costal margin
Aortic aneurysm; above 5 cm usually needs repair

blocks.text: **Spleen vs left kidney.** Spleen: you cannot get above it, it has a notch, it moves down and inward on inspiration, it is not ballottable, it is dull to percussion, and it may have a rub. Kidney: ballottable, and resonant because bowel lies in front of it.

**Courvoisier's law**: a palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient is unlikely to be due to gallstones; think of pancreatic or distal bile duct cancer. A palpable gallbladder has LR+ **26** for obstructed bile ducts in jaundice. But at least half of dilated gallbladders cannot be felt, so its absence does not exclude a non-stone cause.

blocks.title: Ascites at the bedside (LR+ for ascites)
Shifting dullness: technique
items: Flank dullness appears once about **2 litres** of fluid are present. Test shifting dullness only if the flanks are dull
Percuss out to the dull flank and keep your finger on that spot
Roll the patient toward you and wait **30 seconds to 1 minute**
Percuss again. If the spot is now resonant, the test is positive
Mimics: a large ovarian cyst, fluid-filled bowel

blocks.title: Auscultation and the succussion splash
items: Bowel sounds: report as present or absent. **None over 4 minutes** means paralytic ileus. Loud, high-pitched, **tinkling** sounds suggest obstruction. Normal sounds make obstruction unlikely. Kumar notes they are absent in peritonism and otherwise of limited value
Venous hum between xiphisternum and umbilicus: portal hypertension. With dilated abdominal wall veins it is the Cruveilhier–Baumgarten syndrome (cirrhosis)
Arterial **bruit over the liver**: hepatocellular carcinoma or alcoholic hepatitis
Friction rub over liver or spleen: tumour, abscess, recent biopsy, Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome
Succussion splash suggests gastric outlet obstruction. If the patient has just drunk, repeat 4 hours later

blocks.note: Dilated abdominal wall veins; compare costal margin veins, caput Medusae and the IVC obstruction pattern
Grey Turner's sign (flanks) and Cullen's sign (periumbilical) in severe acute pancreatitis
The nine abdominal regions and the four quadrants
Massive splenomegaly; note the splenic notch
Shifting dullness: where dullness and tympany lie when supine and when on the side

sections.title: Completing the exam: groin, rectum and bedside extras

blocks.title: Hernial orifices
items: Examine the patient **standing**
Inguinal hernia: bulges **above** the groin crease. Femoral hernia: at the **medial end** of the crease
In suspected bowel obstruction, look for an incarcerated hernia
If you find a mass, also check the liver, do a rectal exam and feel the supraclavicular nodes

blocks.title: Rectal examination
items: The GI exam is **incomplete without** a rectal exam
Look at the glove for blood, melaena, mucus or pus
Haemorrhoids cannot be felt unless thrombosed. Faeces can be felt but also indent
An empty rectum suggests intestinal obstruction. A loaded rectum suggests constipation
On straining, the perineum normally descends 1–3.5 cm

blocks.title: Finishing off
items: Urinalysis (bilirubin, urobilinogen) and temperature
With cirrhosis or hepatomegaly: sit the patient at 45° and check the JVP (heart failure, constrictive pericarditis)
Feel supraclavicular nodes and look for sacral oedema
If there is ascites, examine the chest for an effusion
Legs: oedema, and skin signs of IBD

blocks.title: After a diagnostic tap: serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG)
rows: Cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, Budd–Chiari, heart failure, constrictive pericarditis
Peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB, pancreatic ascites, nephrotic syndrome

blocks.text: In a patient with cirrhosis and ascites, **abdominal pain, tenderness and fever** suggest **spontaneous bacterial peritonitis**. In about a third, abdominal signs are mild or absent and **fever with encephalopathy** is the main clue.

cards.back: Anaemia, weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, and a palpable abdominal mass

cards.front: New dyspepsia: above what age does Davidson advise endoscopy even without alarm features?

cards.back: Recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week on average over the last 3 months, plus ≥2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form
Severe, constant epigastric or RUQ pain lasting hours, starting unpredictably. It is not truly colicky

cards.front: Colic cycle: small-bowel vs large-bowel obstruction?
cards.back: Small bowel: every 2–3 min, periumbilical. Large bowel: every 10–15 min

cards.front: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start suggests…?
cards.back: A motility disorder such as achalasia (solids only and progressive suggests mechanical obstruction)

cards.front: Diarrhoea that continues during a fast is…?
cards.back: Secretory (high volume, often >1 L/day). Osmotic diarrhoea stops with fasting

cards.front: Dark urine with pale stools means…?
cards.back: Obstructive or cholestatic jaundice: bilirubin is not reaching the gut
Cut down? Annoyed by criticism? Guilty? Eye-opener in the morning?

cards.front: Virchow's node: where, and what does it suggest?
cards.back: Enlarged left supraclavicular node; sentinel node for gastric cancer

cards.front: Which clotting factors fall from vitamin K malabsorption in obstructive jaundice?
Five features that separate the spleen from an enlarged left kidney?
cards.back: Spleen: cannot get above it, notch, moves inferomedially, not ballottable, dull to percussion (± rub). Kidney: ballottable and resonant
Palpable gallbladder + jaundice: probably not gallstones; think pancreatic or distal bile duct cancer

cards.front: Which bedside sign has the highest LR+ for ascites, and how much fluid gives flank dullness?
cards.back: Fluid thrill (LR+ 9.6); flank dullness appears at about 2 litres

cards.front: Direction of flow in dilated veins below the umbilicus: portal hypertension vs IVC obstruction?
cards.back: Portal hypertension: away from the umbilicus (downward). IVC obstruction: upward toward the head
Portal hypertension (cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, Budd–Chiari, heart failure, constrictive pericarditis)

cards.front: Inguinal vs femoral hernia: where is the bulge?
cards.back: Inguinal: above the groin crease. Femoral: at the medial end of the crease

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has had upper abdominal discomfort and bloating after meals for 6 weeks. He has never had these symptoms before. He has no weight loss, vomiting, bleeding or difficulty swallowing, and abdominal examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Non-invasive test for H. pylori and treat if positive
Reassurance and review only if symptoms persist for a year
questions.explanation: Davidson's rule: **new dyspepsia after age 55** needs endoscopy even without alarm features (alarm features would make it urgent). Test-and-treat for H. pylori is the route for younger patients who have no alarm features.
whyNot: Test-and-treat is for patients under 55 with no alarm features; his age alone takes him down the endoscopy route.
Barium studies cannot give a biopsy and are not the first test for dyspepsia.
Ultrasound looks at the biliary tree, not the gastric mucosa where serious disease would be.
New symptoms at his age need investigation, not a long wait.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with schizophrenia develops itching, dark urine and pale stools 3 weeks after a new antipsychotic was started. Her ALP is markedly raised.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Itch, dark urine and pale stools make this a **cholestatic** picture. Chlorpromazine is the classic drug cause of cholestasis, and it is an antipsychotic.
whyNot: Valproate is linked to fatty liver, not cholestasis, and is not her antipsychotic.
Halothane causes hepatitis after anaesthesia.
Amiodarone is linked to fatty liver.
Paracetamol in overdose causes hepatic necrosis, not a cholestatic illness weeks into treatment.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has had 3 months of food sticking behind his sternum. It began with meat, now includes bread, and soup still goes down easily. He has lost 7 kg.
items.explanation: Solids only, getting **progressively** worse, with weight loss: a mechanical, malignant obstruction. Alarm features need urgent endoscopy.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man with asthma and hay fever has needed hospital removal of a food bolus twice this year. Between episodes he swallows normally.
items.explanation: Intermittent bolus impaction in an **atopic** young man is the classic history of eosinophilic oesophagitis. Biopsies are needed even if the mucosa looks normal.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman had a stroke a month ago. She coughs as soon as she tries to swallow, and drinks sometimes come back through her nose.
items.explanation: Trouble **starting** a swallow, choking and **nasal regurgitation** place the problem in the oropharynx; after a stroke it is neurological.

questions.theme: Sources of GI bleeding from the history
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 21-year-old man vomits clear fluid repeatedly after a night of binge drinking. After several bouts of retching, a streak of fresh blood appears in the vomit. He is haemodynamically stable.
items.explanation: Clear vomiting first, then blood after **repeated retching**, is the pattern of a Mallory–Weiss tear.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman takes naproxen daily for knee osteoarthritis. She has passed black, sticky, foul-smelling stools for 2 days and feels faint on standing. She has had no abdominal pain.
items.explanation: Two steps: black tarry stool means **melaena**, so the source is upper GI. Then an NSAID user with an upper GI bleed most likely has a peptic (often duodenal) ulcer, which may be **painless**.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has had looser stools for 4 months, dark blood mixed through the stool and 5 kg weight loss. He had a regular bowel habit all his life before this.
items.explanation: A **new change in bowel habit** in an older patient, blood **mixed into** the stool and weight loss all point to colorectal cancer.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has extensive bruising. His prothrombin time is prolonged.
questions.leadIn: Which clotting factor is NOT reduced by failing hepatic synthesis?
questions.explanation: The liver makes all the clotting factors **except factor VIII**, which is produced elsewhere. Failing synthesis therefore spares factor VIII.
whyNot: Factor II (prothrombin) is made in the liver and falls in cirrhosis.
Factor VII is made in the liver and falls early.
Factor IX is made in the liver and needs vitamin K.
Factor X is made in the liver and needs vitamin K.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has 4 months of upper abdominal discomfort, feeling full after a few mouthfuls and 8 kg weight loss. He has conjunctival pallor. A hard lymph node is felt in the left supraclavicular fossa.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A hard **left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node** is the sentinel node for gastric cancer. Early satiety can be a symptom of stomach cancer, and weight loss and anaemia are alarm features.
whyNot: A duodenal ulcer does not spread to lymph nodes or cause a hard supraclavicular node.
Chronic pancreatitis causes pain and malabsorption, not a hard supraclavicular node.
HCC usually arises in a cirrhotic liver and is not linked with Virchow's node.
Reflux is benign; weight loss and a hard node are alarm features against it.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has dilated veins over the lower abdomen. When you empty a segment below the umbilicus and release it, blood refills from below, flowing up toward the chest.
items.explanation: Upward flow below the umbilicus means the blood is bypassing a blocked **IVC**. In portal hypertension, flow runs away from the umbilicus, so below it the flow is downward.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man who drinks heavily has had 2 days of severe epigastric pain going through to his back. There is bluish discoloration over both flanks.
items.explanation: Flank bruising is **Grey Turner's sign**. With pain through to the back in a heavy drinker, this means severe acute pancreatitis.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a large left upper quadrant mass. You cannot get above it, a notch is felt on its medial edge, it is dull to percussion, and it moves down and inward when he breathes in.
items.explanation: No upper edge, a notch, inferomedial movement and dullness are the features of the **spleen**. A kidney would be ballottable and resonant.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has a tender lump in the left groin. With her standing, the bulge lies at the medial end of the groin crease.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely type of hernia?
questions.explanation: A femoral hernia bulges at the **medial end** of the groin crease, whereas inguinal hernias bulge **above** it. Examine hernial orifices with the patient standing.
whyNot: Inguinal hernias, direct or indirect, bulge above the groin crease.
Indirect inguinal hernias also bulge above the crease, along the inguinal canal.
An incisional hernia arises through an abdominal scar, not at the groin crease.
An epigastric hernia bulges in the epigastric region of the abdominal wall, not at the groin crease.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has tense ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 16 g/L.
questions.leadIn: Which cause best fits this result?
questions.explanation: A SAAG **above 11 g/L** means portal hypertension. Of these options only cirrhosis causes portal hypertension.
whyNot: Peritoneal cancer gives a low SAAG (below 11 g/L).
TB peritonitis gives a low SAAG.
Nephrotic syndrome gives a low SAAG.
Pancreatic ascites gives a low SAAG.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with years of ulcer-type pain now vomits large amounts several hours after meals, sometimes including food eaten the day before. A splash is heard when his abdomen is shaken.
items.explanation: Vomiting long after meals, **old food** in the vomit and a **succussion splash** together point to gastric outlet obstruction, here probably from scarring by a chronic ulcer.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has felt sick and vomited each morning before breakfast for 3 weeks. She is otherwise well. Her last period was 7 weeks ago.
items.explanation: Early-morning vomiting **before food** suggests pregnancy, alcohol or raised ICP. A late period makes pregnancy the obvious first answer.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman says she "vomits" after most meals. Within minutes of eating, food comes back into her mouth effortlessly, and she chews and swallows it again.
items.explanation: Effortless return of food into the mouth after eating, which is then spat out or swallowed again, is **rumination**, not vomiting.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man smokes and has diabetes. He reports "heartburn" that comes on walking uphill and spreads to his left arm and jaw. It has no link to meals or lying down.
items.explanation: Two steps: the "heartburn" is triggered by **exertion**, not by meals or posture. It also **radiates to the arm and jaw**. Treat it as myocardial ischaemia until proven otherwise.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman woke at 2 a.m. with severe, steady pain in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. It lasted 3 hours, then settled. She is now pain-free and has no fever.
items.explanation: "Biliary colic" is a **constant** severe pain lasting hours that starts unpredictably and settles. If the pain persisted with RUQ tenderness, that would suggest cholecystitis.

questions.stem: You are examining a 60-year-old man with a distended abdomen and suspect ascites.
questions.leadIn: Which bedside sign has the highest positive likelihood ratio for ascites?
questions.explanation: Fluid thrill has the highest LR+ (**9.6**), ahead of shifting dullness (5.8). Flank dullness and bulging flanks are sensitive but much weaker as positive findings.
whyNot: Shifting dullness is useful (LR+ 5.8) but below fluid thrill.
Flank dullness has LR+ 2.6; it is mainly a screen before testing for shifting dullness.
Bulging flanks have the lowest LR+ (2.4).
Ankle oedema has LR+ 2.8 and is not an abdominal sign.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with coffee-ground vomiting and melaena. His blood urea is markedly raised but his creatinine is normal.
questions.leadIn: What does this biochemical pattern most likely indicate?
options: A lower GI source of bleeding
questions.explanation: Blood in the upper gut is digested and absorbed as protein, so **urea rises while creatinine stays normal**. This points to a severe upper GI bleed.
whyNot: Chronic kidney disease would raise creatinine as well as urea.
Acute tubular necrosis raises creatinine too.
Vomiting alone does not usually give such an isolated rise in urea, and he has melaena.
Blood from a lower source is not digested and absorbed in the same way; melaena also points upward.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man with cirrhosis has prominent veins around the umbilicus. A continuous humming sound is heard between the xiphisternum and the umbilicus.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for this sound?
questions.explanation: A **venous hum** in this area means portal hypertension. Together with dilated abdominal wall veins in cirrhosis it forms the Cruveilhier–Baumgarten syndrome.
whyNot: An aneurysm gives an expansile epigastric pulsation, not a continuous venous hum.
HCC gives an arterial bruit over the liver itself.
IVC obstruction gives dilated veins with upward flow, not a hum.
Renal artery stenosis gives a bruit lateral to the midline, not a venous hum.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has 3 years of crampy lower abdominal pain on 2 or 3 days most weeks. The pain eases after she opens her bowels. On bad days her stools are looser and more frequent. Her weight is stable, she has no rectal bleeding or nocturnal symptoms, and examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: She meets **Rome IV**: weekly pain over more than 3 months, linked to defecation, with changes in stool frequency and form. She has **no alarm features**, so IBS can be diagnosed positively from the history.
whyNot: Crohn's would be more likely with weight loss, bleeding, nocturnal symptoms or abnormal signs.
Coeliac disease tends to cause malabsorption and weight loss rather than pain eased by defecation.
Cancer is unlikely in a 38-year-old with a 3-year stable course and no alarm features.
Pancreatic pain is epigastric, goes to the back and is not eased by defecation.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man who drinks a bottle of spirits a day has 12 hours of steady epigastric pain going through to his back. He is sitting forward on the trolley and has vomited several times.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1, **character**: the pain is steady, not colicky. Step 2, **site and radiation**: epigastric, going through to the back (pancreas or a penetrating ulcer). Step 3, **relieving factor**: sitting forward is the classic pancreatic posture. Step 4, **associated features**: vomiting is common in pancreatitis, and heavy alcohol use is a risk factor. Everything points to acute pancreatitis.
whyNot: Perforation pain starts abruptly and leaves the patient lying still with a rigid abdomen; it is not eased by sitting forward.
Biliary pain is RUQ or epigastric and usually not eased by sitting forward.
Reflux gives retrosternal burning related to meals and posture, not severe pain through to the back.
SBO gives periumbilical colic every 2–3 minutes with distension.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has a left upper quadrant mass. It is ballottable bimanually, you can get your hand above it, and the percussion note over it is resonant.
questions.leadIn: What is the mass most likely to be?
options: Faecal mass in the splenic flexure
questions.explanation: Work through the spleen-versus-kidney checklist. (1) **Can you get above it?** Yes, so not spleen. (2) **Ballottable?** Yes, which fits a kidney. (3) **Percussion**: resonant, because colon lies in front of the kidney; the spleen is dull. Three points for the kidney, none for the spleen.
whyNot: You cannot get above a spleen, it is dull to percussion and not ballottable.
The left lobe of the liver lies in the epigastrium, is dull and is continuous with the liver.
A gastric cancer is an epigastric mass and is not ballottable like a kidney.
Faeces can be indented and are not ballottable.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has 12 hours of worsening abdominal pain. He lies very still because moving hurts. The abdominal wall is rigid and stays tense despite reassurance and distraction. Bowel sounds are absent.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation: Step 1, **behaviour**: lying still points to peritonitis; rolling about points to colic. Step 2, **muscle tone**: rigidity that does not relax with reassurance is involuntary, which means peritonitis, not guarding. Step 3, **auscultation**: a silent abdomen fits peritonism. All three agree.
whyNot: Obstruction gives colic with restlessness and loud, tinkling bowel sounds.
Ureteric colic makes patients restless and does not cause rigidity.
Voluntary guarding relaxes with reassurance; this did not.
IBS does not cause rigidity or a silent abdomen.

questions.theme: Diarrhoea and change in bowel habit
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman in hospital develops profuse watery diarrhoea 5 days after finishing a course of antibiotics for pneumonia.
items.explanation: Recent **antibiotics** followed by diarrhoea: think C. difficile first.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man came back from trekking abroad a month ago. Since then he has had bloating, wind and loose stools.
items.explanation: Diarrhoea after **travel** suggests Giardia.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man passes bulky, pale, very offensive stools that float and are hard to flush. He has lost weight despite a good appetite.
items.explanation: Pale, floating, foul, hard-to-flush stools are fatty. Weight loss despite a good appetite points to **malabsorption**.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man in intensive care is having more than 1.5 litres of watery stool a day, and it continues unchanged while he is nil by mouth.
items.explanation: High volume that **continues while fasting** is secretory diarrhoea. Osmotic diarrhoea would stop when feeding stops.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman strains at stool, feels blocked at the anus, and sometimes uses a finger to help empty her rectum. Her stool frequency is normal.
items.explanation: Straining, a feeling of blockage and **self-digitation** suggest a pelvic floor evacuation disorder rather than slow transit.

questions.theme: Peripheral signs in GI and liver disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with heavy periods has spoon-shaped nails, cracks at the corners of her mouth and a smooth tongue.
items.explanation: Koilonychia, angular cheilitis and atrophic glossitis together point to **iron deficiency**.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis has white, opaque nail beds on most fingers and pitting oedema to the knees.
items.explanation: Leuconychia (Terry's nails) reflects **hypoalbuminaemia**, which also explains the oedema.

items.stem: An 18-year-old man has a tremor, abnormal liver tests and a golden-brown ring at the edge of each cornea.
items.explanation: Kayser–Fleischer rings in a young person with liver disease mean **Wilson's disease**.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has 2 months of bloody diarrhoea. He also has painful, red, tender nodules on both shins.
items.explanation: Erythema nodosum (and pyoderma gangrenosum) on the legs points to **IBD**.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with painless jaundice, dark urine and pale stools has started bruising easily. Her platelet count is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: pale stools mean bile is not reaching the gut, so this is **obstructive** jaundice. Without bile, fat-soluble vitamin K is poorly absorbed, so factors II, VII, IX and X fall. The platelet count is normal, so thrombocytopenia is not the cause.

questions.stem: You are teaching a student to examine for ascites.
questions.leadIn: Roughly how much free fluid must be present before the flanks become dull to percussion?
questions.explanation: Flank dullness appears once **about 2 litres** of ascites are present. Smaller amounts are easily missed clinically. Test shifting dullness only if the flanks are dull.
whyNot: 200 mL is far too little to change the percussion note.
500 mL cannot be detected reliably by percussion.
1 litre is still usually below the threshold for flank dullness.
Flank dullness appears well before 5 litres; by that volume ascites is usually obvious.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus.
questions.leadIn: In which direction does blood flow in these veins below the umbilicus?
options: Away from the midline laterally only
questions.explanation: In portal hypertension, blood leaves the portal system through umbilical collaterals and flows **away from the umbilicus**. Below it, that means downward. Upward flow below the umbilicus suggests IVC obstruction.
whyNot: Upward flow below the umbilicus is the IVC obstruction pattern.
Flow runs away from the umbilicus, not toward it.
Portal collaterals radiate away from the umbilicus; flow is not purely lateral.
The direction is consistent and is the reason for testing it.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has 18 hours of right upper quadrant pain and a temperature of 38.2 °C. As you press below the right costal margin and ask her to breathe in deeply, she stops breathing in abruptly because of pain.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is **Murphy's sign**: the inflamed gallbladder moves down onto the examiner's hand during inspiration. Persistent RUQ pain with fever fits cholecystitis following biliary pain.
whyNot: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back, not a positive Murphy's sign.
Hepatitis may make the liver tender, but does not stop inspiration in this way.
Perforation gives sudden severe pain with generalised peritonism.
Ureteric colic gives loin-to-groin colic and restlessness.

questions.theme: Jaundice and chronic liver disease: putting history and signs together
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, pick the best-fitting option from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Carcinoma of the head of pancreas

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has 6 weeks of painless, deepening jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and 8 kg weight loss. A smooth, non-tender mass is felt below the right costal margin and moves with breathing.
items.explanation: Two steps: dark urine and pale stools mean **obstructive** jaundice. A palpable gallbladder with jaundice makes gallstones unlikely (Courvoisier). That leaves a malignant distal obstruction, most often pancreatic.

items.stem: A 53-year-old woman has itched over her arms and legs for a year, which is worse at night. She is now mildly jaundiced and has yellow plaques around her eyelids.
items.explanation: Cholestatic itch is often the **first** symptom of PBC. Xanthelasma reflects the raised cholesterol of cholestasis.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis and known ascites now has fever, diffuse abdominal tenderness and new confusion.
items.explanation: Abdominal pain, tenderness and fever in a cirrhotic patient with ascites suggest **SBP**; encephalopathy may be the main clue when abdominal signs are mild.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with long-standing hepatitis C cirrhosis has lost weight. A bruit is heard over an irregular, enlarged liver.
items.explanation: An **arterial bruit over the liver** suggests HCC (or alcoholic hepatitis). Weight loss in a cirrhotic patient adds to the concern.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has had several short bouts of mild jaundice. His urine stays a normal colour. His mother had her spleen removed and his uncle had gallstones at 25.
items.explanation: Jaundice with **normal-coloured urine** suggests excess unconjugated bilirubin, as in haemolysis. A family history of splenectomy and early gallstones supports a hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has 2 months of difficulty swallowing. Food sticks behind her lower sternum. She has lost 3 kg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first investigation?
options: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor
questions.explanation: Dysphagia always needs **urgent** investigation, and endoscopy is the first test because it allows **biopsy** (and dilatation). Biopsies are taken even if the mucosa looks normal. Talley notes that a barium swallow is sometimes done first to guide endoscopy, but follow Davidson: endoscopy is the investigation of choice.
whyNot: Barium or videofluoroscopy comes after endoscopy, or first for oropharyngeal dysphagia.
Manometry is for suspected motility disorders once a structural lesion is excluded.
CT stages a known cancer; it does not replace endoscopy and biopsy.
A PPI trial without investigation is not acceptable with dysphagia and weight loss.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man asks how much alcohol is considered low risk. You use current UK guidance in your answer.
questions.leadIn: What is the recommended maximum regular weekly intake?
questions.explanation: UK guidance (DoH 2016) is **no more than 14 units a week** for both men and women, spread over 3 or more days.
whyNot: 7 units is below the guideline limit.
21 units is above the current 14-unit weekly limit.
28 units is double the current limit.
35 units is well above the low-risk limit.

ospe.identify: Dilated abdominal wall veins. Caput Medusae (portal hypertension): flow runs away from the umbilicus. IVC obstruction: flow below the umbilicus runs upward
Grey Turner's sign (flank discoloration) and Cullen's sign (periumbilical discoloration) in severe acute pancreatitis; Cullen's sign can also occur with haemoperitoneum
Label the nine abdominal regions (right and left hypochondrium, epigastrium, right and left lumbar, umbilical, right and left iliac fossa, hypogastrium) and the four quadrants
Leuconychia (Terry's nails, from hypoalbuminaemia) and palmar erythema: peripheral signs of chronic liver disease
Asterixis (arms outstretched, wrists extended; flapping tremor of hepatic encephalopathy) and petechiae (thrombocytopenia)
Shifting dullness: the dull flank becomes resonant after the patient rolls toward the examiner, as fluid moves to the dependent side
Massive splenomegaly with a palpable notch; the spleen enlarges toward the right iliac fossa and you cannot get above it
